concept.name: Heteroskedasticity
concept.definition: A violation of the constant-error-variance assumption in regression in which the conditional variance of the disturbance varies across observations, typically as a function of the regressors or of time. OLS coefficients remain unbiased under heteroskedasticity but are no longer efficient, and conventional standard errors are biased.
concept.intuition: The size of the model's mistakes is not constant: errors may balloon for large values of a regressor or in turbulent periods, so treating every observation as equally precise is wrong.
concept.mechanics: Detected by plotting squared residuals against fitted values or regressors and by formal tests such as Breusch-Pagan (regress squared residuals on the regressors and test joint significance) or White's test. Remedies include heteroskedasticity-consistent (White/Huber) standard errors, generalized least squares, or explicit variance models.
concept.formula: Var(epsilon_i | x_i) = sigma_i^2 != sigma^2; in the Breusch-Pagan test, e_i^2 is regressed on x_i and nR^2 of that regression is asymptotically chi-squared under homoskedasticity.
concept.failure_modes: Ignoring heteroskedasticity invalidates t- and F-tests and confidence intervals even though point estimates stay unbiased; in finance, volatility clustering makes homoskedastic inference badly overconfident.
concept.misconceptions: That heteroskedasticity biases the coefficient estimates: it does not; it corrupts inference (standard errors) and efficiency, not the unbiasedness of OLS.
concept.example: A regression of household consumption on income shows residual spread widening with income; a Breusch-Pagan test on squared residuals rejects constant variance, so White standard errors are reported instead.
